title: Version control
plain: Version control is a system that records the saved states of a project's files, with who made each one and when. It lets you compare versions and return to an earlier one.
check: Your app worked at 5 pm and broke at 6 pm. What would you need to have done at 5 pm to be able to find out what changed since then?
rubric: Says it can show what changed between 5 pm and now
Says it can bring back the 5 pm state
Says the 5 pm state must have been recorded on purpose (committed); nothing is recorded automatically
try: Check that Git, the most common version-control tool, is installed: run `git --version`. It prints one line such as `git version 2.54.0`; your number may differ. If you see 'command not found' or 'is not recognized', Git is not installed yet.
pitfall: Many people think version control saves every edit automatically, like cloud sync. It keeps only the states you record on purpose (commits); edits made since the last commit are not in the history.

title: Repository
plain: A repository (repo) is a project folder that Git tracks. Its whole history is stored in a hidden folder named .git inside the project.
check: What makes a folder a Git repository, and how would you see that for yourself?
rubric: Runs git status and reads 'On branch ...' (a repository) or 'fatal: not a git repository' (not one)
Lists hidden items and points to the .git folder
Says the history lives in .git, not in the visible files
try: Open a terminal in your project folder and run `git status`. Inside a repository it starts with `On branch` and the branch name; elsewhere it prints `fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git`. Then show hidden items: `ls -a` (macOS, Linux, Git Bash) or `dir -Force` (PowerShell) and find the `.git` entry.
pitfall: Many learners think the repository is the GitHub website. A repository is a folder on your own computer; GitHub only stores another copy of it.

title: git init
plain: git init turns the current folder into a Git repository by creating a hidden .git folder. Add -b main to name the first branch main.
check: You are about to run git init for your recipe project. How do you make sure you run it in the right folder?
rubric: Runs the command inside the project folder, not in the home or Desktop folder
Runs git init -b main and sees 'Initialized empty Git repository in'
Runs git status and sees 'On branch main' and 'No commits yet'
try: In a practice place: `mkdir git-try`, `cd git-try`, then `git init -b main`. Git prints `Initialized empty Git repository in` followed by the path of a new `.git` folder. Run `git status`: it starts with `On branch main` and says `No commits yet`. The folder is only for practice.
pitfall: Many people expect the first branch to be called main. Git 2.x still calls it master unless you pass -b main (needs Git 2.28 or newer) or set init.defaultBranch; the Git manual says the default will change to main with Git 3.0.

title: The four places
plain: Git keeps your work in four places. They are the working folder (your files), the staging area (changes picked for the next commit), the local repository (saved history) and the remote (a copy elsewhere).
check: After git commit succeeds, which of the four places hold the new snapshot and which do not yet?
rubric: Says the new snapshot is in the local repository, and that the staging area and the working folder match it if nothing was edited afterwards
Says the remote does not have it until git push
Says an edit made after git add is not in the commit and shows as modified in git status
try: In a practice repository with a tracked file, run `git status -s` at each step. After you edit and save the file it shows ` M notes.txt`. After `git add notes.txt` it shows `M  notes.txt`. After `git commit -m "Edit notes"` it prints nothing. The first letter describes the staging area and the second letter describes the working folder.
pitfall: Many people think git add saves their work, or that git commit uploads it. git add only copies a change into the staging area, git commit records it in your local repository, and only git push sends it to a remote.

title: git status
plain: git status shows the state of your project. It lists the current branch, the files that changed, the changes staged for the next commit and the files Git does not track yet.
check: git status lists the same file under 'Changes to be committed' and under 'Changes not staged for commit'. How can one file be in both lists?
rubric: Says 'Changes to be committed' lists staged changes and 'Changes not staged for commit' lists edits made after or without staging
Explains that a file is in both lists when it was staged and then edited again; the commit would contain only the staged version
Identifies 'Untracked files' as files Git has never recorded and uses the hint lines (git add, git restore) to name a next command
try: In a repository, create a file named `notes.txt` in your editor and save it. Run `git status`: the file appears under `Untracked files`. Run `git status -s` for the short form, which shows `?? notes.txt`. Read the hint lines in the long form; they name the next command.
pitfall: A line such as 'Your branch is up to date with origin/main' does not mean your edits are on GitHub. git status does not contact the remote; it compares your commits with your last fetch, and uncommitted edits never count.

title: Staging (git add)
plain: Staging means choosing which changes go into your next commit. git add <file> copies the file's current content into the staging area; nothing is saved to the history until you commit.
check: You changed five files but want one commit about only two of them. How do you make sure the commit contains exactly those two?
rubric: Runs git add with a specific file name, not git add . or git add -A
Runs git status and shows one file under 'Changes to be committed' and the other under 'Changes not staged for commit'
Reads git diff --staged to see exactly what the commit would contain
try: In a repository with two changed files, run `git add one-file.txt` (use a real file name), then `git status`: only that file appears under `Changes to be committed`. To take it out of the staging area again, run `git restore --staged one-file.txt`; this does not touch the contents of the file.
pitfall: git add . and git add -A are fast, but they stage everything that is not ignored, including a .env file or a build folder you forgot to ignore. Name the files you mean (or use git add -p) and read git status first.

title: Commit
plain: A commit is a saved snapshot of your project, made from the staging area. It is stored in your local repository with a message, an author and a time. You can return to it later.
check: After you run git commit -m "Add notes", what do you expect git status to print, and why?
rubric: Runs git status first and commits only what was intended
Runs git commit -m with a message, sees the commit id, and predicts that git status now says 'nothing to commit, working tree clean'
Runs git log --oneline and sees the new commit at the top
try: In a practice repository: create `notes.txt` in your editor, run `git add notes.txt`, then `git commit -m "Add notes file"`. Git prints a line such as `[main (root-commit) 4f3d043] Add notes file` and `1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)`; your id differs. Then `git status` says `nothing to commit, working tree clean`. If Git says `Author identity unknown`, set your name and e-mail first (see the identity card).
pitfall: A commit is not the same as saving a file: saving writes the file to disk, while a commit records a snapshot of the staged changes in Git's history. The commit also stays on your computer until you push it.

title: Commit messages
plain: A good commit message starts with a short line (about 50 characters or fewer) that says what the change does, in command form such as 'Add login form'. A longer body can explain why.
check: What would you write as the message for your last change, so that someone who reads git log in six months understands it?
rubric: The first line is about 50 characters or fewer and starts with a verb such as Add, Fix or Remove
It names what changed, not only that something changed
A body line explains why when the reason is not obvious
try: In a practice repository, change a file and commit it with a message such as `Add recipe page with ingredient list`. Run `git log --oneline` and check that the new line reads like a sentence about the change. If a message needs more than one line, run `git commit` without -m; Git opens your editor. If an unfamiliar editor opens (often Vim), press Esc, type `:q!` and press Enter to leave without committing.
pitfall: Messages like 'wip' or 'fix' feel fine today, but the log is how you find a change later. A good message says what changed and, when it is not obvious, why; and it never contains secrets or personal data, because history is permanent.

title: git log
plain: git log lists the commits of the current branch, newest first, with each commit's id, author, date and message. git log --oneline shows one short line per commit.
check: git log --oneline prints '4f3d043 Add notes file'. What is 4f3d043 good for?
rubric: Runs git log --oneline -n 3 and reads the ids and messages
Opens one commit with git show <id>, names the file that changed, and says the id is what other commands (git show, git revert, git switch -c) use to name that commit
Leaves the pager with the q key
try: In a repository with some commits, run `git log --oneline`. Then pick one id from the list and run `git show <id>` to see that commit's changes. If the output fills the screen and stops, you are in a pager; press `q` to leave it.
pitfall: git log shows only committed history: uncommitted edits are not in it, and by default only the commits of the branch you are on. Add --all to see other branches.

title: git diff
plain: git diff shows exactly which lines changed. A line starting with - was removed, a line starting with + was added, and an @@ line says where in the file the change is.
check: You edit a file, run git add on it, then run git diff and see nothing. Why is the output empty?
rubric: Says that - marks the old line and + marks the new line
Says that the @@ line gives line numbers for the old and the new version of the changed block
Knows that git diff shows unstaged changes and git diff --staged shows staged ones
try: In a repository, change one line of a tracked file in your editor and save it. Run `git diff`: you see a `--- a/...` line, a `+++ b/...` line, an `@@` line and your change with `-` and `+`. Then run `git add <file>`, run `git diff` again (empty), and run `git diff --staged` (shows the change).
pitfall: People read git diff as the history of a file, but it compares only two states: by default the working folder against the staging area, and with --staged the staging area against the last commit. A new untracked file does not appear in it at all.

title: .gitignore
plain: A .gitignore file lists files and patterns that Git should not track, such as .env with secrets or node_modules with downloaded code. It affects only files that Git does not track yet.
check: You committed .env last week, and today you add .env to .gitignore. What does that change, and what is still a problem?
rubric: Says .gitignore does not affect a file that Git already tracks; it needs git rm --cached .env
Says the old commits still contain the key, so the key must be revoked and replaced
Runs git check-ignore -v .env and reads the output (source file, line number, pattern, then the path)
try: In a practice repository, create a file `.env` in your editor with one made-up line such as `KEY=not-a-real-key`. Run `git status -s`: it shows `?? .env`. Create `.gitignore` containing the line `.env`, then run `git check-ignore -v .env`. It prints `.gitignore:1:.env` and the path `.env`, separated by a tab. `git status -s` now lists only `?? .gitignore`.
pitfall: Adding a file to .gitignore does not stop Git tracking a file it already tracks, and it never removes anything from old commits. A tracked secret must be untracked with git rm --cached and replaced with a new one; git check-ignore prints nothing for tracked files.

title: Git name and e-mail
plain: Every commit records an author name and e-mail taken from your Git settings user.name and user.email. Set them once with git config --global. Anyone who can read the repository can see them.
check: Git stops your first commit with 'Author identity unknown'. Which e-mail address would you give it for a public repository, and why?
rubric: Runs git config --global user.name and git config --global user.email with their own values
Uses the GitHub-provided no-reply address (ID+USERNAME@users.noreply.github.com) or an address they accept to make public
Confirms the values with git config --global user.name and git config --global user.email
try: Run `git config --global user.name` and `git config --global user.email`. Each prints your saved value, or nothing if it is not set. To set them: `git config --global user.name "Ada Example"` and `git config --global user.email "12345+ada@users.noreply.github.com"`; use your own name and copy your own no-reply address from the Emails page of your GitHub settings (it is shown when 'Keep my email addresses private' is selected). Skip this step if both commands already print values you like.
pitfall: The name and e-mail in Git are only text written into each commit; they are not a login, and Git does not check them. Changing them affects future commits only: older commits keep the address they were made with.

title: Remote and origin
plain: A remote is another copy of your repository stored elsewhere, usually on a site such as GitHub. origin is the name Git gives the remote you cloned from.
check: git remote -v prints nothing. What does that tell you about the project?
rubric: Runs git remote -v
Says that origin is only a name and the address after it is where the copy lives
Says that no output means the project has no remote yet
try: In any repository, run `git remote -v`. A cloned project prints two lines, one marked `(fetch)` and one marked `(push)`, with the same address. A project made with `git init` prints nothing, which is normal: it has no remote yet.
pitfall: People think origin is GitHub or a special keyword, but it is only a nickname for an address that you can rename or add to. Git talks to a remote only when you run clone, fetch, pull or push.

title: git push
plain: git push uploads your new local commits to a branch on the remote. Only committed work is sent. The first push of a new branch is usually git push -u origin <branch>.
check: git push says 'Everything up-to-date', but you edited three files today. What did you probably forget to do?
rubric: Reads git status first: uncommitted edits are listed as changes and are not sent, and 'ahead of origin/main by N commits' shows the commits waiting to be sent
Checks that the repository is private, or that making this work public is intended, before the first push
Runs git push -u origin main (first time) or git push and reads the output
try: Before you push for real, run `git push --dry-run`. It sends nothing and shows what would be sent, for example `main -> main`. A branch that has no upstream yet stops with `fatal: The current branch ... has no upstream branch` and prints the command to use; then run `git push --dry-run -u origin main` instead. If the result looks right and the repository is yours and private, run the same command without --dry-run (`git push`, or `git push -u origin main` the first time).
pitfall: Many learners think git push sends all their saved files, or that it works with the GitHub account password. It sends only committed work, and GitHub asks for a personal access token or a browser sign-in (for example through Git Credential Manager), not the account password.

title: git clone
plain: git clone downloads a full copy of a remote repository, with all its history, into a new folder on your computer and names the source origin.
check: Why should you not run git clone inside a folder that is already a Git repository?
rubric: Says that cloning inside a repository creates a repository inside a repository: the outer one lists it as one untracked folder and warns about an embedded repository on git add
Runs git clone <address> from a folder that is not inside a repository, then moves into the new folder named after the repository
Runs git log --oneline and git remote -v to show the history and origin
try: In an empty practice folder that is not inside any project, run `git clone https://github.com/octocat/Hello-World.git` (GitHub's small public demo repository). Git prints `Cloning into 'Hello-World'...`. Then `cd Hello-World`, run `git log --oneline` and `git remote -v` to see the history and the origin address.
pitfall: A clone is not a ZIP download: it brings the whole history and keeps the link to origin, so you can fetch and push later. It does not bring files that were never committed or are ignored, such as a .env file that exists only on the original computer.

title: fetch vs pull
plain: git fetch downloads new commits from the remote and stores them as origin/main, leaving your files alone. git pull runs a fetch and then combines the new commits into your current branch.
check: A friend pushed a commit to main and you run git fetch. What has changed on your computer, and what has not?
rubric: Says that git fetch changes none of your files and only updates origin/main
Says that git status afterwards reports that the branch is behind origin/main by 1 commit
Says that git pull then brings that commit into the current branch (a fast-forward or a merge)
try: Inside a cloned repository run `git fetch`. If nothing is new it prints nothing; if something is new it prints a line such as `abc1234..def5678  main -> origin/main`. Then run `git status`: it says whether your branch is behind, ahead or has diverged. To see the incoming commits before combining them, run `git log HEAD..origin/main --oneline`.
pitfall: git pull is not only a download: it is fetch plus combining. If you and the remote both have new commits, Git stops with 'Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches' until you choose merge, rebase or fast-forward only.

title: Branches
plain: A branch is a named line of commits for work apart from main. In Git it is only a movable name that points to one commit, so creating a branch is instant.
check: You create a branch called try-colors but do not switch to it, and then you make a commit. Which branch gets the commit, and why?
rubric: Runs git branch and recognises the * as the branch you are on
Creates a branch with git branch <name> and lists it with git branch -vv
Explains that two branches point to the same commit until one of them gets a new commit
try: In a practice repository with at least one commit, run `git branch`: a list with `*` next to the current branch. Run `git branch try-colors`, then `git branch -vv`: both branches show the same commit id. Remove the practice branch with `git branch -d try-colors`; Git refuses if it holds commits that no other branch has.
pitfall: A branch is not a copy of the folder: there is still one working folder, and switching branches changes its files to match the branch. Creating a branch does not move you onto it.

title: Switching branches
plain: git switch <branch> moves you to another branch and changes the files in your folder to match it. git switch -c <name> creates a new branch first. Older guides use git checkout for this.
check: You edited a file but did not commit, and you run git switch main. What are the two things that can happen?
rubric: Uses git switch -c <name> and sees 'Switched to a new branch'
Predicts the two outcomes for uncommitted edits: they come along to main if nothing conflicts, or Git refuses to switch and lists the files
Reads the current branch name from git status
try: In a practice repository run `git switch -c try-colors`. Edit a file, save it and commit it. Run `git switch main` and open the file: the old text is back. Run `git switch try-colors`: your change is back. Git prints `Switched to a new branch` or `Switched to branch` each time.
pitfall: Uncommitted edits do not belong to a branch: they travel with you when you switch, or Git refuses to switch if they would be overwritten. Older tutorials use git checkout for this job and for restoring files; Git 2.23 added git switch and git restore to separate them.

title: git merge
plain: git merge <branch> brings the commits of another branch into the branch you are on. Only your current branch changes; the other branch stays as it was.
check: You are on main and run git merge try-colors. Which branch changes, and which one stays exactly as it was?
rubric: Switches to the branch that should receive the changes (main) first
Runs git merge <branch> and tells a 'Fast-forward' from a merge commit in the output
Runs git log --oneline --graph and reads the shape of the history
try: In a practice repository with a branch that has one extra commit, run `git switch main`, then `git merge try-colors --no-edit` (the option stops an editor window from opening). If main had no new commits since you branched, the output contains `Fast-forward`; otherwise Git creates a merge commit. Then run `git log --oneline --graph`. Delete the practice folder when you are done.
pitfall: Merging is not symmetric. git merge X changes only the branch you are on, and X is not deleted afterwards. People often merge in the wrong direction because they did not check git status first.

title: Merge conflicts
plain: A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines. Git writes both versions into the file between <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>. You choose what to keep, remove the markers and commit.
check: A conflicted file shows `<<<<<<< HEAD`, one line, `=======`, another line and `>>>>>>> theme-red`. Which line comes from the branch you are on, and which from the other branch?
rubric: Says the lines between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= come from the branch they are on, and the lines below ======= up to >>>>>>> theme-red come from the other branch
Finds the conflicted file with git status ('both modified') and edits it so that no marker line remains and the content is what was intended
Runs git add <file> and git commit, and git status says the working tree is clean
try: In an empty practice folder: `git init -b main`, create `site.txt` containing `color: blue`, then `git add site.txt` and `git commit -m "Add site"`. Run `git switch -c theme-red`, change the line to `color: red` and `git commit -am "Red"`. Run `git switch main`, change the line to `color: green` and `git commit -am "Green"`. Run `git merge theme-red --no-edit`: Git prints `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in site.txt`. Open the file, keep one line, delete the three marker lines, then run `git add site.txt` and `git commit --no-edit`. To give up instead, run `git merge --abort`.
pitfall: A conflict is not damage: Git needs you to decide, and git merge --abort puts everything back as it was before the merge. The usual mistake is committing with the marker lines still in the file, which breaks the code.

title: Undo uncommitted changes
plain: git restore <file> discards your uncommitted edits in that file and puts back the staged or last committed version. Git never recorded those edits, so they cannot be recovered.
check: You edited notes.txt for an hour without committing and then run git restore notes.txt. What happens to your hour of edits?
rubric: Says that git restore notes.txt permanently discards the unstaged edits in that file
Says that git restore --staged notes.txt only removes the change from the staging area and keeps the edit in the file
Says that committed work is not touched by either command
try: Practise the safe half in your project: run `git add notes.txt`, then `git status` (the file is under `Changes to be committed`), then `git restore --staged notes.txt`, then `git status` again (the file is back under `Changes not staged for commit`, and its content is unchanged). Try plain `git restore notes.txt` only on a practice file you do not mind losing.
pitfall: People expect an undo or a recycle bin. git restore discards uncommitted edits with no way back, because Git only keeps what was staged or committed. Read git diff first, and commit or stash when you are unsure.

title: git revert
plain: git revert <commit> adds a new commit that undoes the changes of an earlier commit. The old commit stays in the history, so revert is safe even for commits you already pushed.
check: You pushed a commit that broke the site, and teammates already pulled it. Why is git revert a safer way to undo it than deleting the commit?
rubric: Finds the commit id with git log --oneline
Runs git revert <id> with a clean working folder
Shows the original commit and a new 'Revert' commit in git log, and the file content as it was before
try: In a practice repository, make a small commit, then run `git revert --no-edit HEAD`. Git prints a line such as `[main ae497e2] Revert "Add line3"`. Run `git log --oneline`: the new Revert commit is on top and your file is back as before. The working folder must be clean (`git status`) before you start.
pitfall: People think undoing a commit means deleting it. revert deletes nothing: it adds a second commit that cancels the first. To revert a merge commit you must also say which parent to keep with -m.

title: git reset
plain: git reset moves the current branch back to an earlier commit. --soft keeps the changes staged, --mixed (the default) keeps them as edits, and --hard also discards all uncommitted changes in your files.
check: You have two hours of uncommitted edits and one commit you regret. What is the difference for your edits between git reset --soft HEAD~1 and git reset --hard HEAD~1?
rubric: Soft: the branch moves; the staging area and files keep the changes
Mixed (the default): the branch and the staging area move; the files keep the edits
Hard: branch, staging area and files all match the target commit, so uncommitted edits are lost
try: In a practice repository with at least two commits, run `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, then `git status`: the changes of the last commit are now staged. Run `git commit -m "Redo"` to make the commit again. Do not practise --hard on work you care about.
pitfall: Many people treat reset --hard as a tidy undo, but it overwrites your files and discards every uncommitted edit with no way back. For commits you already pushed, use revert instead of reset plus a force push.

title: git reflog
plain: git reflog lists where HEAD (the commit you are on) pointed recently on your computer, including commits that a reset or a deleted branch left behind. Entries last for weeks.
check: After git reset --hard HEAD~2 you realise you needed those two commits. Where could you find them again?
rubric: Runs git reflog and finds the entry from before the reset by its message
Gets the commit back with git switch -c rescued <id> or git reset --hard <id>
Says that uncommitted edits were never recorded, so the reflog cannot bring them back
try: In a practice repository with three commits, run `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, then `git reflog`. The top lines show `reset: moving to HEAD~1` and, directly below, the commit you lost as `HEAD@{1}` with its message. Copy its id and run `git switch -c rescued <id>`; the lost commit is on the new branch.
pitfall: People think a reset or a deleted branch destroys committed work, but the commits usually stay reachable through the reflog for weeks (by default 90 days, or 30 days for commits no branch points to). Uncommitted edits were never recorded, so the reflog cannot bring them back.

title: git stash
plain: git stash sets your uncommitted changes aside and returns your files to the last commit. git stash pop brings them back later. Stashes are stored inside your repository.
check: You stash your edits, make a new commit that changes the same lines, and then run git stash pop. What can go wrong?
rubric: Runs git stash and sees 'Saved working directory and index state'; git status is clean and git stash list shows the entry
Runs git stash pop and sees the edit return
Says that pop can stop with a conflict when the same lines changed, and that Git then keeps the stash entry
try: In a practice repository, edit and save a tracked file `notes.txt`, then run `git stash`. Git prints `Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: ...`. Run `git status` (clean) and open the file (original text). Run `git stash list` (shows `stash@{0}`), then `git stash pop` to get your edit back.
pitfall: git stash does not save new, untracked files by default: they stay in the folder, and with only untracked files Git says 'No local changes to save' (add -u to include them). A stash you forget about stays hidden, so check git stash list from time to time.

title: A secret was pushed
plain: If a secret such as an API key or password was ever pushed, treat it as exposed. First revoke or replace it at the provider; cleaning the Git history comes later and is optional.
check: You notice an API key in a file that you pushed to a private repository ten minutes ago. What is the first thing you do, and why before anything in Git?
rubric: Says the key must be revoked or replaced at its provider first, before touching Git
Untracks the file with git rm --cached, adds it to .gitignore and commits
Says that a new commit, deleting the repository or a force push does not make the old key safe
try: Practise with a made-up key only. In a practice repository create `.env` containing `KEY=not-a-real-key`, then `git add .env` and `git commit -m "Add env"`. Next run `git rm --cached .env`, put `.env` in `.gitignore`, run `git add .gitignore` and `git commit -m "Stop tracking env"`. Finally run `git log -p --oneline` (press q to leave the pager) and find the made-up key in the first commit: deleting a file later does not remove it from old commits.
pitfall: Deleting the file in a new commit, deleting the repository or force-pushing does not make a leaked key safe, because clones, forks and cached views may still hold it. Revoke or replace the key first.
